does: Turns chocolate or a solid fat liquid over gentle heat, without letting it colour, scorch or seize.

intro.what: Melting gently turns chocolate or solid fat into a smooth liquid without browning it.
intro.why: It teaches you to use gentle heat and residual warmth rather than overheating the last solid pieces.

how: Chop chocolate into small, even pieces, and cut butter into cubes.
Set a bowl over a pan of barely simmering water, with the bottom of the bowl clear of the water.
Stir now and then, and take the bowl off while a few small lumps are left. They melt as you stir.
Butter on its own can be melted in a small pan over low heat.

cues.text: Smooth and glossy, with no lumps and no grainy streaks.
Barely warm to the touch, never hot.

mistakes.mistake: Letting steam or a drop of water into chocolate, which makes it seize into a stiff, grainy paste.
mistakes.fix: Keep the bowl and the spoon dry, and the water at a bare simmer.

mistakes.mistake: Heating chocolate straight on the flame or too fast, so that it scorches and turns thick and bitter.
mistakes.fix: Melt it over water, and off the heat for the last lumps.

quiz.question: What distinguishes gentle melting from browning?
choices: The solids develop a deep nut-brown colour.
The surface chars before the centre softens.
The solid becomes liquid without colouring or scorching.
quiz.because: Melting aims for a smooth liquid while keeping browning and scorching out of the process.

quiz.question: When should you take melting chocolate off the warm water?
choices: While small lumps remain, then stir them in.
Only after heating the smooth liquid strongly.
After the chocolate becomes thick and smoky.
quiz.because: Residual warmth melts the last small lumps without unnecessary additional heat.

quiz.question: Which appearance matches melted chocolate?
choices: Smooth and glossy without grainy streaks.
Dark scorched patches in a thick mass.
quiz.because: A smooth glossy liquid shows melting without seizing or scorching.

quiz.question: A little water has made the chocolate seize. What would you change next time?
choices: Let more steam condense into the bowl.
Use a stronger flame directly under the chocolate.
Keep bowl and spoon dry and the water at a bare simmer.
quiz.because: Water entering chocolate can cause seizing; dry tools and gentle indirect heat avoid that mistake.
